nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-02.title: Multiple of six
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-02.body:
The number of students must be a multiple of $6$ greater than $1000$; the smallest is $6\cdot167=1002$.

**Answer: 1002**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-03.title: Set up the ratio
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-03.body:
Let $AZ=x$. Since $A$ is between $Z$ and $B$, $ZB=x+12$. Then $\frac{x}{x+12}=\frac23$, so $3x=2x+24$ and $x=24$.

**Answer: 24**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-04.title: Pair the outer and inner factors
Difference of squares
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-04.body:
If $N$ is the root, $N^2-1=(N-1)(N+1)=(100\cdot103)(101\cdot102)=10300\cdot10302$. These two factors differ by $2$, so $N-1=10300$ and $N=10301$.

**Answer: 10301**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-05.title: Teacher-days
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-05.body:
The job took $1+2+3=6$ teacher-days. Three teachers working together do $3$ teacher-days per day, so they would need $2$ days.

**Answer: 2 days**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-06.title: Use the smallest cubes
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-06.body:
A number is divisible by a cube greater than $1$ exactly when it is divisible by the cube of a prime: $8, 27, 125, \dots$. Up to $81$ only $8$ and $27$ matter, and two consecutive numbers cannot both be multiples of $8$, so we need a multiple of $8$ next to a multiple of $27$. The multiples of $27$ up to $81$ are $27, 54, 81$: $27,54$ have neighbours $26,28,53,55$, none divisible by $8$; $81$ has neighbour $80=8\cdot10$. Hence the pair is $80,81$ ($80=2^4\cdot5$, $81=3^4$).

**Answer: 80 and 81**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-07.title: Right trapezoid
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-07.body:
Since $\angle N$ and $\angle L$ are right angles, $MN\parallel LQ$ and $MNLQ$ is a right trapezoid. Drop $QT\perp MN$; then $QLNT$ is a rectangle, $NT=LQ=x$, $MT=2x-x=x$, and $QT=LN=x-2$. From $\tan M=\frac{QT}{MT}=\frac{x-2}{x}=\frac23$ we get $x=6$. In right triangle $LNQ$, $QN^2=LN^2+LQ^2=4^2+6^2=52$, so $QN=2\sqrt{13}$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{13}$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-08.title: Including the trivial square
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-08.body:
$1=1^2$ is a perfect square and leaves remainder $1$ when divided by $19$, so it is the smallest. (The original key gave $324$, the smallest such square greater than $1$: $N^2-1=(N-1)(N+1)$ divisible by $19$ forces $N\equiv\pm1\pmod{19}$, giving $N=18$ next. The league's correction letter changed the answer to $1$.)

**Answer: 1**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-09.title: Track the water
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-09.body:
Mix $a$ gallons of Chablee (water fraction $\frac13$) with $b$ gallons of Zinfoundel (water fraction $\frac15$) to get water fraction $\frac14$: $\frac a3+\frac b5=\frac{a+b}4$, i.e. $20a+12b=15a+15b$, so $5a=3b$. With $a=9$, $b=15$, and the total is $24$ gallons.

**Answer: 24 gallons**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-09.title: Alligation
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-09.body:
The water fractions are $\frac13$ and $\frac15$, and the target is $\frac14$. The distances are $\frac13-\frac14=\frac1{12}$ and $\frac14-\frac15=\frac1{20}$, so the amounts must be in the inverse ratio $a:b=\frac1{20}:\frac1{12}=3:5$. Thus $9$ gallons of Chablee needs $15$ of Zinfoundel: $24$ gallons.

**Answer: 24 gallons**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-11.title: Diameters and right angles
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-11.body:
Label the vertices so that $E$ is opposite $P$; $PE=10$ is a diameter. The vertices on one side pair up symmetrically: the chords from $P$ to a vertex $V$ and to the vertex $V'$ symmetric to $V$ about the perpendicular bisector of $PE$ have squares that add to $PE^2$: the reflection swaps $P$ and $E$, so $PV'=EV$, and $PV^2+EV^2=PE^2$ because $\angle PVE=90^\circ$ (angle in a semicircle). Each side of $PE$ has four vertices forming two such pairs, giving $2\cdot100$ per side. Total: $200+200+100=500$.

**Answer: 500**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-11.title: Vectors
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-11.body:
Place the center at the origin. For a vertex $V$, $|PV|^2=|P|^2+|V|^2-2P\cdot V=50-2P\cdot V$. Summing over all ten vertices (including $P$ itself, which contributes $0$), $\sum V=0$, so the sum is $10\cdot50=500$.

**Answer: 500**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-12.title: Count with logs
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-12.body:
A number with $N$ digits lies in $[10^{N-1},10^N)$. Here $\log_{10}2^{100}=100\cdot0.3=30$, so $N-1\le30<N$ and $N=31$. (Indeed $2^{100}\approx1.27\times10^{30}$.)

**Answer: 31**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-13.title: Square and check
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-13.body:
Squaring: $6-4x-x^2=x^2+8x+16$, so $2x^2+12x+10=0$ and $x=-1$ or $x=-5$. For $x=-5$ the right side is $-1<0$, so it is extraneous. For $x=-1$: $\sqrt{6+4-1}=3=x+4$. The only solution is $x=-1$.

**Answer: $-1$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-14.title: Count committees
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-14.body:
Committees containing all three friends: $\binom{27}{7}$; all committees: $\binom{30}{10}$. The ratio is $\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8}{30\cdot29\cdot28}=\frac{720}{24360}=\frac{6}{203}$.

**Answer: $\frac{6}{203}$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-14.title: One friend at a time
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-14.body:
The first friend is chosen with probability $\frac{10}{30}$; given that, the second with $\frac9{29}$; then the third with $\frac8{28}$. Product: $\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8}{30\cdot29\cdot28}=\frac6{203}$.

**Answer: $\frac{6}{203}$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-15.title: Add a multiple of 13
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-15.body:
$n^2-8n+4$ is a multiple of $13$ exactly when $n^2-8n+4+13n=n^2+5n+4=(n+1)(n+4)$ is. Since $13$ is prime, $13\mid n+1$ or $13\mid n+4$, so $n\equiv12$ or $9\pmod{13}$. The two smallest are $9$ and $12$, with sum $21$.

**Answer: 21**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-16.title: Rectangle overlap
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-16.body:
$BC$ and $EF$ are opposite, parallel sides of the hexagon, directly across from each other, at distance $CE=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}{2}=\sqrt3$. Each square extends $1$ unit inward from its side, so together they cover $2$ units across a gap of $\sqrt3$; they overlap in a $1\times(2-\sqrt3)$ rectangle, of area $2-\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $2-\sqrt3$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-17.title: Compare angles at A
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-17.body:
$\angle BAC=180^\circ-60^\circ-39^\circ=81^\circ$, so $\angle BAX=27^\circ$. In right triangle $BAT$, $\angle BAT=90^\circ-60^\circ=30^\circ$. Hence $\angle XAT=30^\circ-27^\circ=3^\circ$.

**Answer: $3^\circ$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-18.title: Doubling
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-18.body:
If the first term is $a$, the terms are $a$, $a+1$, $2a+2$, $4a+4,\dots$: from the third term on, each term is twice the previous one (the new partial sum plus one is the old term plus the old term). So the $n$th term is $2^{n-2}(a+1)$ for $n\ge2$, and $2^8(a+1)=1280$ gives $a+1=5$, $a=4$.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-20.title: Find the side
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-20.body:
Let the octagon side be $x$; each cut triangle has hypotenuse $x$ and legs $\frac{x}{\sqrt2}$. Along a side of the square: $\frac{x}{\sqrt2}+x+\frac{x}{\sqrt2}=1$, so $x(1+\sqrt2)=1$ and $x=\sqrt2-1$. The four cut triangles fit together into a square of side $x$, so the octagon's area is $1-x^2=1-(3-2\sqrt2)=2\sqrt2-2$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt2-2$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-21.title: Factor
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-21.body:
$2\sin x+6\sin x\cos x=2\sin x(1+3\cos x)=0$. $\sin x=0$ gives $x=0,\pi,2\pi$; $\cos x=-\frac13$ gives two more values in $(\frac\pi2,\pi)$ and $(\pi,\frac{3\pi}2)$. Total: $5$.

**Answer: 5**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-22.title: Work down from the largest squares
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-22.body:
A remainder is less than the divisor. Trying squares from the top: $1000=484\cdot2+32=441\cdot2+118=400\cdot2+200=361\cdot2+278=324\cdot3+28=289\cdot3+133$. Every remaining square is $256$ or less, so its remainder is less than $278$. The largest remainder is $278$.

**Answer: 278**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-23.title: Diameter
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-23.body:
The radius to the point of tangency $T$ is perpendicular to $BC$, so the center lies on $AT$; since $A$ is also on the circle, $AT$ is a diameter. In right triangle $ATC$ with $\angle C=45^\circ$, $AT=20\sin45^\circ=10\sqrt2$. The radius is $5\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $5\sqrt2$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-24.title: Sum to product
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-24.body:
$(\sin7x+\sin13x)+(\sin9x+\sin11x)=2\sin10x\cos3x+2\sin10x\cos x=2\sin10x(\cos3x+\cos x)=4\sin10x\cos2x\cos x$. The smallest positive zeros of the factors are $\frac\pi{10}$, $\frac\pi4$, $\frac\pi2$, so the answer is $\frac{\pi}{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{\pi}{10}$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-25.title: Farthest point
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-25.body:
The tangent length from $X$ to circle $O$ is $\sqrt{XO^2-16}$, largest when $XO$ is largest. Since $O$ lies on $PT$ with $PO=10-4=6$, $XO\le XP+PO=16$, with equality when $X$ is diametrically opposite $T$. Then the tangent length is $\sqrt{256-16}=\sqrt{240}=4\sqrt{15}$.

**Answer: $4\sqrt{15}$**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-26.title: Even exponents
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-26.body:
A perfect-square divisor has even exponents: $2^{0,2,4,6}$ (4 choices), $3^{0,2,4}$ (3), $5^0$ (1), $7^{0,2}$ (2), $11^{0,2}$ (2). Total $4\cdot3\cdot1\cdot2\cdot2=48$.

**Answer: 48**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-28.title: Linear cost
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-28.body:
Meeting $x$ miles from New York costs $10\cdot10x+5\cdot10(150-x)=50x+7500$ cents, smallest at $x=0$: $7500$ cents $=75$ dollars.

**Answer: 75 dollars**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-28.title: Majority argument
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-28.body:
Moving the meeting one mile toward New York saves $10$ people's mile and costs $5$ people's mile, so it always helps; meet in New York. Then $5$ people travel $150$ miles at \$0.10: $5\cdot150\cdot0.10=75$ dollars.

**Answer: 75 dollars**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-29.title: Factor
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-29.body:
$x^3-6x^2+11x-6=(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)$, which is zero exactly at $x=1,2,3$. The smallest positive integer where it is nonzero is $4$.

**Answer: 4**

nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-30.title: Chords as sines
nyciml-1989-90-spring-seniora-30.body:
Put the polygon in a circle of diameter $1$, so a chord subtending an inscribed angle $\theta$ has length $\sin\theta$. If each side subtends inscribed angle $x$, then $AB=\sin x$, $AC=\sin2x$, $AD=\sin3x$, and
$$\frac1{\sin x}=\frac1{\sin2x}+\frac1{\sin3x}\iff\sin2x\sin3x=\sin x\sin3x+\sin x\sin2x.$$
Converting products to sums: $\cos x-\cos5x=\cos2x-\cos4x+\cos x-\cos3x$, so $\cos2x+\cos5x=\cos3x+\cos4x$, i.e. $2\cos\frac{7x}2\cos\frac{3x}2=2\cos\frac{7x}2\cos\frac x2$. For a polygon $x<\frac\pi3$, so $\cos\frac{3x}{2}\ne\cos\frac x2$; hence $\cos\frac{7x}2=0$, $x=\frac\pi7$, and the polygon has $\frac{\pi}{x}=7$ vertices.

**Answer: 7**
